sources.title: Our Pasts III, Chapter 7: Women, Caste and Reform
Our Pasts III, Chapter 6: Civilising the Native, Educating the Nation

claims.claim: Two hundred years ago most children were married off at an early age, and both Hindu and Muslim men could marry more than one wife.
claims.quote: Most children were married off at an early age. Both Hindu and Muslim men could marry more than one wife.

claims.claim: Widows who died by burning themselves on their husband's funeral pyre were called sati, meaning virtuous women.
claims.quote: In some parts of the country, widows were praised if they chose death by burning themselves on the funeral pyre of their husbands. Women who died in this manner, whether willingly or otherwise, were called "sati", meaning virtuous women.

claims.claim: Women's rights to property were restricted and most women had virtually no access to education.
claims.quote: Women's rights to property were also restricted. Besides, most women had virtually no access to education.

claims.claim: In many parts of the country people believed that if a woman was educated, she would become a widow.
claims.quote: In many parts of the country people believed that if a woman was educated, she would become a widow.

claims.claim: Brahmans and Kshatriyas considered themselves upper castes; below them came Vaishyas, then peasants and artisans (Shudras).
claims.quote: Brahmans and Kshatriyas considered themselves as "upper castes". Others, such as traders and moneylenders (often referred to as Vaishyas) were placed after them. Then came peasants, and artisans such as weavers and potters (referred to as Shudras).

claims.claim: The groups at the bottom were treated as untouchable: barred from temples, wells and ponds used by upper castes.
claims.quote: They were not allowed to enter temples, draw water from the wells used by the upper castes, or bathe in ponds where upper castes bathed.

claims.claim: From the early nineteenth century, print (books, newspapers, magazines, leaflets, pamphlets) made debate far cheaper and more accessible than manuscripts.
claims.quote: For the first time, books, newspapers, magazines, leaflets and pamphlets were printed. These were far cheaper and far more accessible than the manuscripts

claims.claim: Printed debate could reach a wider public and become linked to movements for social change.
claims.quote: The discussions could reach out to a wider public, and could become linked to movements for social change.

claims.claim: Raja Rammohun Roy (1772-1833) founded a reform association known as the Brahmo Sabha (later known as the Brahmo Samaj) in Calcutta.
claims.quote: One such reformer was Raja Rammohun Roy (1772-1833). He founded a reform association known as the Brahmo Sabha (later known as the Brahmo Samaj) in Calcutta.

claims.claim: Reformers are so called because they felt changes were necessary in society and unjust practices needed to be done away with.
claims.quote: People such as Rammohun Roy are described as reformers because they felt that changes were necessary in society, and unjust practices needed to be done away with.

claims.claim: Rammohun Roy was keen to spread Western education and bring about greater freedom and equality for women.
claims.quote: Rammohun Roy was keen to spread the knowledge of Western education in the country and bring about greater freedom and equality for women.

claims.claim: Rammohun began a campaign against sati and tried to show through his writings that widow burning had no sanction in ancient texts.
claims.quote: He began a campaign against the practice of sati. Rammohun Roy was well versed in Sanskrit, Persian and several other Indian and European languages. He tried to show through his writings that the practice of widow burning had no sanction in ancient texts.

claims.claim: By the early nineteenth century many British officials had also begun to criticise Indian traditions and customs.
claims.quote: By the early nineteenth century, as you have read in Chapter 6, many British officials had also begun to criticise Indian traditions and customs.

claims.claim: In 1829, sati was banned.
claims.quote: In 1829, sati was banned.

claims.claim: Reformers' strategy: to challenge a harmful practice, find a verse in the ancient sacred texts supporting their view and argue the present practice was against early tradition.
claims.quote: Whenever they wished to challenge a practice that seemed harmful, they tried to find a verse or sentence in the ancient sacred texts that supported their point of view. They then suggested that the practice as it existed at present was against early tradition.

claims.claim: In Rammohun's published dialogue on sati, the opponent asks when women were ever given a fair opportunity to exhibit their natural capacity.
claims.quote: OPPONENT OF SATI: When did you ever afford them a fair opportunity of exhibiting their natural capacity? How then can you accuse them of want of understanding?

claims.claim: Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar used ancient texts to suggest widows could remarry; a law was passed in 1856 permitting widow remarriage.
claims.quote: For instance, one of the most famous reformers, Ishwarchandra Vidyasagar, used the ancient texts to suggest that widows could remarry. His suggestion was adopted by British officials, and a law was passed in 1856 permitting widow remarriage.

claims.claim: Those against widow remarriage opposed Vidyasagar and even boycotted him.
claims.quote: Those who were against the remarriage of widows opposed Vidyasagar, and even boycotted him.

claims.claim: In the Telugu-speaking areas of the Madras Presidency, Veerasalingam Pantulu formed an association for widow remarriage.
claims.quote: In the Telugu-speaking areas of the Madras Presidency, Veerasalingam Pantulu formed an association for widow remarriage.

claims.claim: Young intellectuals and reformers in Bombay pledged themselves to working for the cause of widow remarriage.
claims.quote: Around the same time, young intellectuals and reformers in Bombay pledged themselves to working for the same cause.

claims.claim: Swami Dayanand Saraswati, founder of the Arya Samaj, also supported widow remarriage.
claims.quote: In the north, Swami Dayanand Saraswati, who founded the reform association called Arya Samaj, also supported widow remarriage.

claims.claim: Yet the number of widows who actually remarried remained low, and those who married were not easily accepted in society.
claims.quote: Yet, the number of widows who actually remarried remained low. Those who married were not easily accepted in society and conservative groups continued to oppose the new law.

claims.claim: Dayanand founded the Arya Samaj in 1875, an organisation that attempted to reform Hinduism.
claims.quote: Dayanand founded the Arya Samaj in 1875, an organisation that attempted to reform Hinduism.

claims.claim: Vidyasagar in Calcutta and many reformers in Bombay set up schools for girls.
claims.quote: Vidyasagar in Calcutta and many other reformers in Bombay set up schools for girls.

claims.claim: When the first girls' schools opened in the mid-nineteenth century, people feared schools would take girls away from home and their domestic duties, and that travelling through public places would corrupt them.
claims.quote: When the first schools were opened in the mid-nineteenth century, many people were afraid of them. They feared that schools would take girls away from home, prevent them from doing their domestic duties. Moreover, girls had to travel through public places in order to reach school. Many people felt that this would have a corrupting influence on them.

claims.claim: Throughout the nineteenth century most educated women were taught at home; Rashsundari Debi secretly learned to read and write by candlelight at night.
claims.quote: Therefore, throughout the nineteenth century, most educated women were taught at home by liberal fathers or husbands. Sometimes women taught themselves. Do you remember what you read about Rashsundari Debi in your book Social and Political Life last year? She was one of those who secretly learned to read and write in the flickering light of candles at night.

claims.claim: In the latter part of the century, schools for girls were established by the Arya Samaj in Punjab and Jyotirao Phule in Maharashtra.
claims.quote: In the latter part of the century, schools for girls were established by the Arya Samaj in Punjab, and Jyotirao Phule in Maharashtra.

claims.claim: Mumtaz Ali reinterpreted verses from the Koran to argue for women's education.
claims.quote: Some reformers such as Mumtaz Ali reinterpreted verses from the Koran to argue for women's education.

claims.claim: The Hindu Mahila Vidyalaya was one of the first institutions to give girls the kind of learning usual for boys.
claims.quote: The Hindu Mahila Vidyalaya was one of the first institutions to provide girls with the kind of learning that was usual for boys at the time.

claims.claim: The Begums of Bhopal founded a primary school for girls at Aligarh.
claims.quote: From the early twentieth century, Muslim women like the Begums of Bhopal played a notable role in promoting education among women. They founded a primary school for girls at Aligarh.

claims.claim: Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain started schools for Muslim girls in Patna and Calcutta.
claims.quote: Another remarkable woman, Begum Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain started schools for Muslim girls in Patna and Calcutta.

claims.claim: Rokeya was a fearless critic of conservative ideas, arguing that religious leaders of every faith accorded an inferior place to women.
claims.quote: She was a fearless critic of conservative ideas, arguing that religious leaders of every faith accorded an inferior place to women.

claims.claim: By the 1880s, Indian women began to enter universities; some trained to be doctors, some became teachers.
claims.quote: By the 1880s, Indian women began to enter universities. Some of them trained to be doctors, some became teachers.

claims.claim: Tarabai Shinde, educated at home at Poona, published Stripurushtulna (A Comparison between Women and Men), criticising social differences between men and women.
claims.quote: Tarabai Shinde, a woman educated at home at Poona, published a book, Stripurushtulna, (A Comparison between Women and Men), criticising the social differences between men and women.

claims.claim: Pandita Ramabai, a great scholar of Sanskrit, felt Hinduism was oppressive towards women and wrote about the miserable lives of upper-caste Hindu women.
claims.quote: Pandita Ramabai, a great scholar of Sanskrit, felt that Hinduism was oppressive towards women, and wrote a book about the miserable lives of upper-caste Hindu women.

claims.claim: Ramabai founded a widows' home at Poona where women were trained so they could support themselves economically.
claims.quote: She founded a widows' home at Poona to provide shelter to widows who had been treated badly by their husbands' relatives. Here women were trained so that they could support themselves economically.

claims.claim: The changes alarmed the orthodox: many Hindu nationalists felt Hindu women adopting Western ways would corrupt Hindu culture and erode family values; orthodox Muslims were also worried.
claims.quote: Needless to say, all this more than alarmed the orthodox. For instance, many Hindu nationalists felt that Hindu women were adopting Western ways and that this would corrupt Hindu culture and erode family values. Orthodox Muslims were also worried about the impact of these changes.

claims.claim: From the early twentieth century women formed political pressure groups to push laws for female suffrage and better health care and education for women.
claims.quote: From the early twentieth century, they formed political pressure groups to push through laws for female suffrage (the right to vote) and better health care and education for women.

claims.claim: In the twentieth century, leaders such as Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose supported demands for greater equality and freedom for women.
claims.quote: In the twentieth century, leaders such as Jawaharlal Nehru and Subhas Chandra Bose lent their support to demands for greater equality and freedom for women.

claims.claim: The Child Marriage Restraint Act was passed in 1929: no man below 18 and no woman below 16 could marry; the limits were later raised to 21 and 18.
claims.quote: In 1929, the Child Marriage Restraint Act was passed without the kind of bitter debates and struggles that earlier laws had seen. According to the Act, no man below the age of 18 and woman below the age of 16 could marry. Subsequently these limits were raised to 21 for men and 18 for women.

claims.claim: Rammohun Roy translated an old Buddhist text that was critical of caste.
claims.quote: Some of the social reformers we have been discussing also criticised caste inequalities. Rammohun Roy translated an old Buddhist text that was critical of caste.

claims.claim: The Prarthana Samaj adhered to the Bhakti tradition that believed in spiritual equality of all castes.
claims.quote: The Prarthana Samaj adhered to the tradition of Bhakti that believed in spiritual equality of all castes.

claims.claim: In Bombay, the Paramhans Mandali was founded in 1840 to work for the abolition of caste.
claims.quote: In Bombay, the Paramhans Mandali was founded in 1840 to work for the abolition of caste.

claims.claim: In secret meetings, reformers would violate caste taboos on food and touch to get rid of the hold of caste prejudice in their lives.
claims.quote: Often, in secret meetings, these reformers would violate caste taboos on food and touch, in an effort to get rid of the hold of caste prejudice in their lives.

claims.claim: During the nineteenth century Christian missionaries began setting up schools for tribal groups and lower-caste children.
claims.quote: There were also others who questioned the injustices of the caste social order. During the course of the nineteenth century, Christian missionaries began setting up schools for tribal groups and "lower"-caste children.

claims.claim: The poor began leaving villages for jobs opening up in the cities - factories and municipalities.
claims.quote: At the same time, the poor began leaving their villages to look for jobs that were opening up in the cities. There was work in the factories that were coming up, and jobs in municipalities.

claims.claim: During the First World War there was a huge demand for shoes for the armies, so traditional leather workers could ask high prices and gain impressive profits.
claims.quote: During the First World War, however, there was a huge demand for shoes for the armies. Caste prejudice against leather work meant that only the traditional leather workers and shoemakers were ready to supply army shoes. So they could ask for high prices and gain impressive profits.

claims.claim: Many Mahar people found jobs in the Mahar Regiment; B.R. Ambedkar's father taught at an army school.
claims.quote: The army, for instance, offered opportunities. A number of Mahar people, who were regarded as untouchable, found jobs in the Mahar Regiment. The father of B.R. Ambedkar, the leader of the Dalit movement, taught at an army school.

claims.claim: In the Bombay Presidency, as late as 1829, untouchables were not allowed into even government schools; when admitted, they sat on the veranda outside the classroom.
claims.quote: In the Bombay Presidency, as late as 1829, untouchables were not allowed into even government schools. When some of them pressed hard for that right, they were allowed to sit on the veranda outside the classroom and listen to the lessons

claims.claim: By the second half of the nineteenth century, people from Non-Brahman castes began organising movements against caste discrimination, demanding social equality and justice.
claims.quote: Gradually, by the second half of the nineteenth century, people from within the Non-Brahman castes began organising movements against caste discrimination, and demanded social equality and justice.

claims.claim: The Satnami movement in Central India was founded by Ghasidas, who worked among the leatherworkers to improve their social status.
claims.quote: The Satnami movement in Central India was founded by Ghasidas who worked among the leatherworkers and organised a movement to improve their social status.

claims.claim: In eastern Bengal, Haridas Thakur's Matua sect worked among Chandala cultivators; Haridas questioned Brahmanical texts that supported the caste system.
claims.quote: In eastern Bengal, Haridas Thakur's Matua sect worked among Chandala cultivators. Haridas questioned Brahmanical texts that supported the caste system.

claims.claim: Shri Narayana Guru of the Ezhava caste proclaimed: oru jati, oru matam, oru daivam manushyanu (one caste, one religion, one god for humankind).
claims.quote: In what is present-day Kerala, a guru from Ezhava caste, Shri Narayana Guru, proclaimed the ideals of unity for his people. He argued against treating people unequally on the basis of caste differences. According to him, all humankind belonged to the same caste. One of his famous statements was: "oru jati, oru matam, oru daivam manushyanu" (one caste, one religion, one god for humankind).

claims.claim: Jyotirao Phule, one of the most vocal low-caste leaders, was born in 1827 and studied in schools set up by Christian missionaries.
claims.quote: One of the most vocal amongst the "low-caste" leaders was Jyotirao Phule. Born in 1827, he studied in schools set up by Christian missionaries.

claims.claim: Phule argued the Aryans were foreigners who defeated and subjugated the true children of the country, then looked at the defeated population as inferior, low-caste people.
claims.quote: Phule argued that the Aryans were foreigners, who came from outside the subcontinent, and defeated and subjugated the true children of the country - those who had lived here from before the coming of the Aryans. As the Aryans established their dominance, they began looking at the defeated population as inferior, as low-caste people.

claims.claim: Phule claimed that before Aryan rule there was a golden age when warrior-peasants tilled the land and ruled the Maratha countryside in just and fair ways.
claims.quote: Phule claimed that before Aryan rule, there existed a golden age when warrior-peasants tilled the land and ruled the Maratha countryside in just and fair ways.

claims.claim: The Satyashodhak Samaj, an association Phule founded, propagated caste equality.
claims.quote: The Satyashodhak Samaj, an association Phule founded, propagated caste equality.

claims.claim: In 1873, Phule wrote a book named Gulamgiri, meaning slavery.
claims.quote: In 1873, Phule wrote a book named Gulamgiri, meaning slavery.

claims.claim: Phule dedicated Gulamgiri to Americans who had fought to free slaves, linking the conditions of India's lower castes with black slaves in America.
claims.quote: Phule dedicated his book to all those Americans who had fought to free slaves, thus establishing a link between the conditions of the "lower" castes in India and the black slaves in America.

claims.claim: Ambedkar was born into a Mahar family; in school he was forced to sit outside the classroom on the ground and could not drink water from taps upper-caste children used.
claims.quote: Ambedkar was born into a Mahar family. As a child he experienced what caste prejudice meant in everyday life. In school he was forced to sit outside the classroom on the ground, and was not allowed to drink water from taps that upper-caste children used.

claims.claim: After finishing school Ambedkar got a fellowship to the US for higher studies; on returning to India in 1919 he wrote extensively about upper-caste power.
claims.quote: After finishing school, he got a fellowship to go to the US for higher studies. On his return to India in 1919, he wrote extensively about "upper"-caste power in contemporary society.

claims.claim: In 1927 Ambedkar started a temple entry movement with his Mahar followers; he led three such movements between 1927 and 1935.
claims.quote: In 1927, Ambedkar started a temple entry movement, in which his Mahar caste followers participated. Brahman priests were outraged when the Dalits used water from the temple tank. Ambedkar led three such movements for temple entry between 1927 and 1935.

claims.claim: Periyar left the Congress in disgust when he found that at a feast organised by nationalists, seating arrangements followed caste distinctions.
claims.quote: Later, he became a member of the Congress, only to leave it in disgust when he found that at a feast organised by nationalists, seating arrangements followed caste distinctions - that is, the lower castes were made to sit at a distance from the upper castes.

claims.claim: Convinced untouchables had to fight for their dignity, Periyar founded the Self Respect Movement.
claims.quote: Convinced that untouchables had to fight for their dignity, Periyar founded the Self Respect Movement.

claims.claim: Periyar was an outspoken critic of Hindu scriptures, especially the Codes of Manu, the Bhagavad Gita and the Ramayana.
claims.quote: Periyar was an outspoken critic of Hindu scriptures, especially the Codes of Manu, the ancient lawgiver, and the Bhagavad Gita and the Ramayana.

claims.claim: Orthodox Hindu society reacted by founding Sanatan Dharma Sabhas and the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal in the north, and the Brahman Sabha in Bengal, to uphold caste distinctions.
claims.quote: But orthodox Hindu society also reacted by founding Sanatan Dharma Sabhas and the Bharat Dharma Mahamandal in the north, and associations like the Brahman Sabha in Bengal. The object of these associations was to uphold caste distinctions as a cornerstone of Hinduism

claims.claim: The Brahmo Samaj, formed in 1830, prohibited all forms of idolatry and sacrifice, believed in the Upanishads, and forbade members from criticising other religious practices.
claims.quote: The Brahmo Samaj: The Brahmo Samaj, formed in 1830, prohibited all forms of idolatry and sacrifice, believed in the Upanishads, and forbade its members from criticising other religious practices.

claims.claim: Keshub Chunder Sen was one of the main leaders of the Brahmo Samaj.
claims.quote: Keshub Chunder Sen - one of the main leaders of the Brahmo Samaj.

claims.claim: Henry Louis Vivian Derozio, a teacher at Hindu College, Calcutta, in the 1820s, promoted radical ideas and encouraged his pupils to question all authority.
claims.quote: Derozio and Young Bengal: Henry Louis Vivian Derozio, a teacher at Hindu College, Calcutta, in the 1820s, promoted radical ideas and encouraged his pupils to question all authority.

claims.claim: Derozio's students, the Young Bengal Movement, attacked tradition and custom, demanded education for women and campaigned for freedom of thought and expression.
claims.quote: Referred to as the Young Bengal Movement, his students attacked tradition and custom, demanded education for women and campaigned for the freedom of thought and expression.

claims.claim: The Ramakrishna Mission, named after Ramakrishna Paramhansa, Vivekananda's guru, stressed salvation through social service and selfless action.
claims.quote: The Ramakrishna Mission and Swami Vivekananda: Named after Ramakrishna Paramhansa, Swami Vivekananda's guru, the Ramakrishna Mission stressed the ideal of salvation through social service and selfless action.

claims.claim: Swami Vivekananda (1863-1902), whose original name was Narendra Nath Dutta, spread Ramakrishna's teachings all over the world.
claims.quote: Swami Vivekananda (1863-1902), whose original name was Narendra Nath Dutta, combined the simple teachings of Sri Ramakrishna with his well founded modern outlook and spread them all over the world.

claims.claim: After hearing Vivekananda at the World Parliament of Religions at Chicago in 1893, the New York Herald reported it was foolish to send missionaries to this learned nation.
claims.quote: After hearing him in the World Parliament of Religions at Chicago in 1893, the New York Herald reported, "We feel how foolish it is to send missionaries to this learned nation".

claims.claim: Vivekananda believed any reform could become successful only by uplifting the condition of the masses.
claims.quote: He firmly believed that any reform could become successful only by uplifting the condition of the masses.

claims.claim: Vivekananda's call to serve the nation made a signal contribution to the nascent nationalism of India.
claims.quote: Therefore, his clarion call to the people of India was to rise above the narrow confines of their 'religion of the kitchen' and come together in the service of the nation. By sending out this call, he made a signal contribution to the nascent nationalism of India.

claims.claim: The Prarthana Samaj, established in 1867 at Bombay, sought to remove caste restrictions, abolish child marriage, encourage women's education and end the ban on widow remarriage.
claims.quote: The Prarthana Samaj: Established in 1867 at Bombay, the Prarthana Samaj sought to remove caste restrictions, abolish child marriage, encourage the education of women, and end the ban on widow remarriage.

claims.claim: The Veda Samaj, established in Madras in 1864, was inspired by the Brahmo Samaj and worked to abolish caste distinctions and promote widow remarriage and women's education.
claims.quote: The Veda Samaj: Established in Madras (Chennai) in 1864, the Veda Samaj was inspired by the Brahmo Samaj. It worked to abolish caste distinctions and promote widow remarriage and women's education. Its members believed in one God.

claims.claim: The Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental College, founded by Sayyid Ahmed Khan in 1875 at Aligarh, later became the Aligarh Muslim University.
claims.quote: The Aligarh Movement: The Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental College, founded by Sayyid Ahmed Khan in 1875 at Aligarh, later became the Aligarh Muslim University. The institution offered modern education, including Western science, to Muslims.

claims.claim: The first Singh Sabhas were formed at Amritsar in 1873 and at Lahore in 1879.
claims.quote: The Singh Sabha Movement: Reform organisations of the Sikhs, the first Singh Sabhas were formed at Amritsar in 1873 and at Lahore in 1879.

claims.claim: Khalsa College, Amritsar, was established in 1892 by the leaders of the Singh Sabha movement.
claims.quote: Khalsa College, Amritsar, established in 1892 by the leaders of the Singh Sabha movement.

claims.claim: The Singh Sabhas sought to rid Sikhism of superstitions, caste distinctions and non-Sikh practices, and promoted education among the Sikhs.
claims.quote: The Sabhas sought to rid Sikhism of superstitions, caste distinctions and practices seen by them as non-Sikh. They promoted education among the Sikhs, often combining modern instruction with Sikh teachings.

claims.claim: Phule was also critical of the anti-colonial nationalism preached by upper-caste leaders.
claims.quote: Phule was also critical of the anti-colonial nationalism that was preached by upper-caste leaders.

claims.claim: In 1927 Ambedkar said his followers wanted to go to the tank only to prove that, like others, they were also human beings.
claims.quote: In 1927, Ambedkar said: "We now want to go to the Tank only to prove that like others, we are also human beings

claims.claim: The British felt they had a cultural mission: to civilise the natives, change their customs and values.
claims.quote: For, the British in India wanted not only territorial conquest and control over revenues. They also felt that they had a cultural mission: they had to "civilise the natives", change their customs and values.

claims.claim: William Jones arrived in Calcutta in 1783 as a junior judge at the Supreme Court; he was a linguist who learnt Sanskrit from pandits.
claims.quote: In 1783, a person named William Jones arrived in Calcutta. He had an appointment as a junior judge at the Supreme Court that the Company had set up. In addition to being an expert in law, Jones was a linguist.

claims.claim: Jones, with Colebrooke and Halhed, set up the Asiatic Society of Bengal and started a journal called Asiatick Researches.
claims.quote: Englishmen like Henry Thomas Colebrooke and Nathaniel Halhed were also busy discovering the ancient Indian heritage, mastering Indian languages and translating Sanskrit and Persian works into English. Together with them, Jones set up the Asiatic Society of Bengal, and started a journal called Asiatick Researches.

claims.claim: Jones and Colebrooke shared a deep respect for ancient cultures, of India and the West, and felt Indian civilisation had attained its glory in the ancient past.
claims.quote: Jones and Colebrooke came to represent a particular attitude towards India. They shared a deep respect for ancient cultures, both of India and the West. Indian civilisation, they felt, had attained its glory in the ancient past, but had subsequently declined.

claims.claim: A madrasa was set up in Calcutta in 1781 to promote the study of Arabic, Persian and Islamic law; the Hindu College was established in Benaras in 1791 to encourage the study of ancient Sanskrit texts.
claims.quote: With this object in view, a madrasa was set up in Calcutta in 1781 to promote the study of Arabic, Persian and Islamic law; and the Hindu College was established in Benaras in 1791 to encourage the study of ancient Sanskrit texts that would be useful for the administration of the country.

claims.claim: Warren Hastings, an enthusiastic supporter of the Orientalists, took the initiative to set up the Calcutta Madrasa.
claims.quote: You will notice that the majestic figure of Hastings, an enthusiastic supporter of the Orientalists, is placed between the standing figure of a pandit on one side and a seated munshi on the other. Hastings and other Orientalists needed Indian scholars to teach them the "vernacular" languages, tell them about local customs and laws, and help them translate and interpret ancient texts. Hastings took the initiative to set up the Calcutta Madrasa

claims.claim: James Mill attacked the Orientalists: the aim of education ought to be to teach what was useful and practical, not to please the natives.
claims.quote: James Mill was one of those who attacked the Orientalists. The British effort, he declared, should not be to teach what the natives wanted, or what they respected, in order to please them and "win a place in their heart". The aim of education ought to be to teach what was useful and practical.

claims.claim: Macaulay saw India as an uncivilised country that needed to be civilised, and held no branch of Eastern knowledge comparable to what England had produced.
claims.quote: By the 1830s, the attack on the Orientalists became sharper. One of the most outspoken and influential of such critics of the time was Thomas Babington Macaulay. He saw India as an uncivilised country that needed to be civilised. No branch of Eastern knowledge, according to him could be compared to what England had produced.

claims.claim: Macaulay declared that a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia.
claims.quote: Who could deny, declared Macaulay, that "a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia".

claims.claim: Following Macaulay's minute, the English Education Act of 1835 made English the medium of instruction for higher education and stopped the promotion of Oriental institutions.
claims.quote: Following Macaulay's minute, the English Education Act of 1835 was introduced. The decision was to make English the medium of instruction for higher education, and to stop the promotion of Oriental institutions like the Calcutta Madrasa and Benaras Sanskrit College.

claims.claim: Wood's Despatch (1854) was issued by Charles Wood, President of the Board of Control, and outlined the educational policy to be followed in India.
claims.quote: In 1854, the Court of Directors of the East India Company in London sent an educational despatch to the Governor-General in India. Issued by Charles Wood, the President of the Board of Control of the Company, it has come to be known as Wood's Despatch. Outlining the educational policy that was to be followed in India

claims.claim: Wood's Despatch said European learning would make Indians recognise the advantages of trade and commerce and create a demand for British goods.
claims.quote: One of the practical uses the Despatch pointed to was economic. European learning, it said, would enable Indians to recognise the advantages that flow from the expansion of trade and commerce, and make them see the importance of developing the resources of the country. Introducing them to European ways of life, would change their tastes and desires, and create a demand for British goods

claims.claim: Wood's Despatch argued European learning would improve Indians' moral character and supply the Company with civil servants who could be trusted.
claims.quote: Wood's Despatch also argued that European learning would improve the moral character of Indians. It would make them truthful and honest, and thus supply the Company with civil servants who could be trusted and depended upon.

claims.claim: In 1857 universities were established in Calcutta, Madras and Bombay.
claims.quote: Following the 1854 Despatch, several measures were introduced by the British. Education departments of the government were set up to extend control over all matters regarding education. Steps were taken to establish a system of university education. In 1857, while the sepoys rose in revolt in Meerut and Delhi, universities were being established in Calcutta, Madras and Bombay.

claims.claim: Until 1813 the East India Company was opposed to missionary activities in India.
claims.quote: Until 1813, the East India Company was opposed to missionary activities in India. It feared that missionary activities would provoke reaction amongst the local population and make them suspicious of British presence in India.

claims.claim: The missionaries set up a mission at Serampore in Danish-controlled territory; a printing press was set up in 1800 and a college established in 1818.
claims.quote: Unable to establish an institution within British-controlled territories, the missionaries set up a mission at Serampore in an area under the control of the Danish East India Company. A printing press was set up in 1800 and a college established in 1818.

claims.claim: William Adam found over 1 lakh pathshalas in Bengal and Bihar, small institutions with no more than 20 students each.
claims.quote: Adam found that there were over 1 lakh pathshalas in Bengal and Bihar. These were small institutions with no more than 20 students each.

claims.claim: The total number of children taught in the pathshalas was over 20 lakh.
claims.quote: But the total number of children being taught in these pathshalas was considerable - over 20 lakh.

claims.claim: The pathshala system was flexible: no fixed fee, no printed books, no separate building, no benches, no blackboards, no separate classes, no roll-call, no annual examinations, no regular timetable.
claims.quote: The system of education was flexible. Few things that you associate with schools today were present in the pathshalas at the time. There were no fixed fee, no printed books, no separate school building, no benches or chairs, no blackboards, no system of separate classes, no roll-call registers, no annual examinations, and no regular timetable.

claims.claim: Adam found the flexible system suited to local needs: classes were not held during harvest time, so even children of peasant families could study.
claims.quote: Adam discovered that this flexible system was suited to local needs. For instance, classes were not held during harvest time when rural children often worked in the fields. The pathshala started once again when the crops had been cut and stored. This meant that even children of peasant families could study.

claims.claim: After 1854 the Company decided to improve vernacular education by introducing order, routines, rules, inspections, textbooks and annual examinations; aided pathshalas got grants, others got no support.
claims.quote: After 1854, the Company decided to improve the system of vernacular education. It felt that this could be done by introducing order within the system, imposing routines, establishing rules, ensuring regular inspections.

claims.claim: By the mid-nineteenth century, schools for girls were being set up by Christian missionaries and Indian reform organisations.
claims.quote: By the mid-nineteenth century, schools for girls were being set up by Christian missionaries and Indian reform organisations.

claims.claim: Serampore College stands on the banks of the river Hooghly near Calcutta; William Carey helped establish the Serampore Mission.
claims.quote: Fig. 6 - William Carey was a Scottish missionary who helped establish the Serampore Mission. Fig. 7 - Serampore College on the banks of the river Hooghly near Calcutta.

claims.claim: In aristocratic Muslim households in North India, women learnt to read the Koran in Arabic, taught by women who came home to teach.
claims.quote: In aristocratic Muslim households in North India, women learnt to read the Koran in Arabic. They were taught by women who came home to teach.

claims.claim: The Non-Brahman sects tried to change habits that provoked the contempt of dominant castes and to create a sense of self-esteem among the subordinate castes.
claims.quote: They tried to change those habits and practices which provoked the contempt of dominant castes. They tried to create a sense of self-esteem among the subordinate castes.

claims.claim: In the early twentieth century the non-Brahman movement started, initiated by non-Brahman castes that had acquired education, wealth and influence, who argued Brahmans were heirs of Aryan invaders.
claims.quote: In the early twentieth century, the non-Brahman movement started. The initiative came from those non-Brahman castes that had acquired access to education, wealth and influence. They argued that Brahmans were heirs of Aryan invaders from the north

claims.claim: From the early nineteenth century many Indian thinkers talked of the need for a wider spread of education; some, impressed by Europe, urged the British to open more schools, colleges and universities.
claims.quote: From the early nineteenth century, many thinkers from different parts of India began to talk of the need for a wider spread of education. Impressed with the developments in Europe, some Indians felt that Western education would help modernise India. They urged the British to open more schools, colleges and universities, and spend more money on education.
